quarterly_data.signal: CFO: Q2 consolidated revenue was NT$33.1 hundred million versus NT$25.9 hundred million in Q1, up 28% QoQ and better than the original guidance of high-single-digit growth. Mass production (MP) was the main growth engine, up 48% QoQ to NT$24.3 hundred million, back above NT$20 hundred million; IP was steady at NT$4.3 hundred million; NRE fell 16% QoQ to NT$4.5 hundred million because revenue-recognition timing was deferred, but was still up 9.5% YoY. Gross margin was 45.2% versus 47.3% in Q1, down 2.1 points, mainly because MP's share of revenue rose from 63% to 73%.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 revenue NT$33.1 hundred million, +28% QoQ (guided high single digit); MP NT$24.3 hundred million, +48% QoQ; gross margin 45.2%; MP share 63% -> 73%

quarterly_data.signal: CEO (president): H1 2026 revenue was NT$59 hundred million; excluding last year's large customer material-procurement revenue, H1 grew about 30%. MP is about 70% of revenue. Within MP, MCU revenue grew about 90% to NT$16.7 hundred million in H1, nearly doubling and almost equal to all of last year, while ASIC MP rose 16% to NT$24.5 hundred million, with demand from US and Japanese customers rising noticeably. H1 IP revenue was NT$8.5 hundred million, up 22%, helped by IP build-out demand for UMC's 12nm. The CEO said Q2 MP growth came from three forces at once: pricing (foundry and OSAT cost increases passed through, raising unit prices), capacity scarcity, and higher demand, including customers ordering early ahead of price increases, restocking from low inventories and raising safety stock.
quarterly_data.figure: H1 revenue NT$59 hundred million (~30% growth excluding material-procurement revenue); H1 MCU MP NT$16.7 hundred million (~90%); H1 ASIC MP NT$24.5 hundred million (+16%); H1 IP NT$8.5 hundred million (+22%)

quarterly_data.signal: CFO guidance for Q3 2026: consolidated revenue to decline by a single-digit percentage QoQ, with IP growing and NRE and MP declining; gross margin flat at around 45%; operating expenses up by a single-digit percentage QoQ. CFO: full-year 2026 NRE is still expected above NT$20 hundred million, and MP is expected to stay above NT$20 hundred million per quarter in the coming quarters. CEO: the Q3 dip mainly reflects customers pulling in shipments in Q2 for fear of price increases, a normal seasonal adjustment; the full-year revenue target is unchanged - excluding customer material-procurement revenue, 2026 revenue can still grow about 10% or more. IP momentum is strong: royalties benefit as foundry capacity is mostly fully loaded and wafer prices rise, so Q3 IP revenue has a chance to set a quarterly record and full-year IP an annual record; NRE depends on the pace of revenue recognition.
quarterly_data.figure: Q3 revenue down single-digit % QoQ; gross margin ~45%; opex up single-digit % QoQ; 2026 growth ~10% or more excluding material-procurement revenue; 2026 NRE above NT$20 hundred million; MP above NT$20 hundred million per quarter

quarterly_data.signal: CEO: mature-node supply has moved from cyclical swings to an irreversible structural tightening - 8-inch and 12-inch mature capacity has become a strategic resource, global capacity expansion lags demand, and shortages of labour, materials or capacity are the new normal, so foundry pricing has long-term support rather than being a short-lived phenomenon. Faraday's value is shifting from design technology (now only the entry ticket) to full value-chain management: capacity booking, wafer allocation, packaging and test capacity coordination and cost management. On 2027: mature-node capacity for Q4 2026 is already very full and will squeeze into Q1 2027 for both 8-inch and 12-inch; management expects next year to be as tight as this year and, given the UMC relationship, sees Faraday benefiting as it did during the pandemic, with a higher chance of securing capacity - calling it the best timing for Faraday.
quarterly_data.figure: mature-node 8-inch and 12-inch capacity full in Q4 2026, squeezing into Q1 2027; no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: CEO: most of the advanced-packaging mass production originally planned for H2 2026 has been deferred to next year. Reasons: customer-supplied SoC dies arrive too slowly (validation problems, some needing re-spins that take another three to six months); one customer's HBM procurement has slowed; and OSAT capacity, especially engineering resources, is tighter and supports Faraday less than expected. Customers understand and will not easily cancel the related orders, and the packaging capacity booked for them is kept. Advanced packaging will miss this year's plan, but MCU and mature-node ASIC MP make up for it, so the full-year revenue target can still be met; the CEO remains positive on next year. Timelines: when the customer supplies the SoC die, MP used to take about a year and now more than a year, even two; when Faraday designs the die, MP takes at least two years. Management expects 2 to 3 such projects in 2027 and most of the packaging projects to reach mass production next year. On OSAT capacity favouring large customers, the CEO said the projects will reach MP smoothly but with longer lead times, citing decades of cooperation with the OSATs and capacity booked as a package with customers.
quarterly_data.figure: most H2 2026 advanced-packaging MP deferred to 2027; 2 to 3 projects expected in 2027; no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: CEO: advanced-node and advanced-packaging project intake is steady; complex NRE SoC designs have long lead times, so this does not yet show in NRE revenue, but the pipeline under negotiation is more positive. With engineering resources limited and supply-chain capacity tight, Faraday now focuses on higher-value projects. It is pursuing several cloud-related advanced-node projects; in communications it targets OCS switches among others, and in Q2 it won a project in an OCS switch, with other cases in progress. Revenue contribution is still small and many projects expected to enter MP may slip into next year. The customer base is shifting quickly toward US and European customers, which lifts margins. Under tight capacity, OSATs are less willing to support small-volume, engineering-heavy projects, so Faraday targets higher-quality projects to win OSAT support.

CEO on the nearly three-year Intel Foundry collaboration: phase one was 18A validation - Faraday taped out an 18A test chip last year, validating the process kit and building physical-design experience. Phase two: Intel now promotes 18A-P (an upgraded 18A) to outside customers; 18A is for Intel's internal use while 18A-P is open to external foundry partners. Faraday has downloaded the 18A-P PDK 1.1, completed the internal environment setup with the reference flow running, and is porting its ecosystem to 18A-P. Phase three is winning real design-service / turnkey projects: this month Faraday reached a milestone, providing design services to an Intel Foundry partner to implement 18A-P - the amount is not yet large, but it is a real implementation. Faraday holds regular meetings with Intel roughly every one to two weeks.
quarterly_data.figure: 18A test chip taped out last year; 18A-P PDK 1.1 set up; first 18A-P design-service engagement, amount not large

quarterly_data.signal: CEO on the UMC-Intel 12nm collaboration: the first revenue benefit for Faraday is 12nm IP development (IP licensing), followed by 12nm ASIC. Management describes the 12nm fab as US-based with scale and geographic advantages, making local production and the North American market easier to address. Faraday's IP is built almost entirely on UMC 14nm and will be replicated to the Intel 12nm node quickly; it expects to start engaging UMC 12nm customers in the second half of next year. The playbook mirrors 28nm, where Faraday has taken on 100+ chips: owning its IP makes its NRE quotes very competitive. On IP licensing, 12nm is the main driver (high unit price, and a new node needs a full build from foundation IP to function IP); with 18A-P and the UMC 12nm process, Faraday expects two strong new product lines from next year.
quarterly_data.figure: UMC 12nm customer engagement from H2 next year; 100+ chips taken at 28nm; no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: CEO on consolidated MCU subsidiary Artery: Q2 revenue NT$9.63 hundred million, up 47% QoQ and 102% YoY, a quarterly record; gross margin 40%, up 5 points from 35% on the pricing mechanism and product mix; opex NT$1.99 hundred million, up 24% QoQ and 58% YoY, mainly cash-settled employee equity compensation for China staff (Chinese regulations prevent the share scheme); operating income up 170% QoQ and 494% YoY to NT$1.86 hundred million, a record; net income NT$1.75 hundred million, up 157% QoQ and 629% YoY; EPS NT$2.79. Under a hybrid ASIC plus MCU model, semi-custom needs are served with Artery MCUs and full custom with ASICs, and Artery's sales channels can also sell Faraday products.
quarterly_data.figure: Artery Q2 revenue NT$9.63 hundred million (+47% QoQ, +102% YoY); gross margin 40%; operating income NT$1.86 hundred million; net income NT$1.75 hundred million; EPS NT$2.79

quarterly_data.signal: CEO: Artery's 2026 outlook is raised - at the last call management said full-year revenue could grow more than 60% with Q2 the peak; now Q3 should grow again rather than decline and full-year revenue should more than double, with gross margin held above 40%. Q3 opex will be the year's highest (equity compensation plus most of the year's bonus cost booked in Q3); the China employee equity compensation is recognised over three years, highest this year, lower next year and lower again the year after. Drivers cited: with strong UMC support Artery began building inventory late last year, so it has more product on hand than peers; prices were raised in H1 to pass on shortages and supply-chain costs and will be raised again in July, especially as memory costs keep rising; a foundry-made MCU needs at least six to nine months from order to product; high-end 32-bit MCUs grow faster than traditional 8-bit parts. Artery's design-win project count this year is a record, which feeds next year's revenue, so management sees next year as positive, with figures to come next quarter.
quarterly_data.figure: Artery 2026 revenue to more than double (earlier: more than 60% growth); gross margin above 40%; Q3 opex the year's peak; further price increase in July

quarterly_data.signal: CEO: robotics was 6% of Artery's 2025 revenue and rose to 8% in H1 2026, with robotics revenue nearly doubling YoY. Artery is designed into more than ten humanoid-robot models (volumes still small); a dexterous hand needs nearly 20 MCUs and a humanoid 50 to 70; a drone needs one MCU per rotor (four for four rotors) plus flight control and gimbal. Artery also sells into mowing, window-cleaning (selling very well), floor-cleaning, educational, companion and industrial robots. High oil prices have lifted demand for light electric vehicles (e-bikes, scooters, electric motorcycles) and energy-storage equipment. Robots, drones and 3D printers need high-end MCUs that 8-bit parts cannot serve.
quarterly_data.figure: robotics 6% of Artery 2025 revenue -> 8% in H1 2026; 10+ humanoid models; ~20 MCUs per dexterous hand, 50 to 70 per humanoid

contracts.signal: CEO: with 8-inch and 12-inch mature-node capacity tight into Q1 2027, Faraday's relationship with UMC gives it a higher chance of securing capacity, as during the pandemic; MCU subsidiary Artery's capacity access was backed by strong UMC support.
